power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: The DSM-5 Mixed Features Specifier: A Clinical Construct Hard to Find

text.text: The DSM-5 mixed features specifier excludes irritability, psychomotor agitation, and distractibility from the diagnostic criteria for mixed depression, deeming them non-specific symptoms that overlap with pure major depressive episodes.
This exclusionary decision has created significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

Empirical evidence demonstrates that DSM-5 criteria identify only 0-12% of depressed patients with mixed features, compared with 33-47% when broader criteria inclusive of agitation and irritability are applied.
These excluded symptoms are not incidental; they are the most prevalent features of clinically observed mixed depression.
The exclusion of these core symptoms sits in tension with both clinical observation and Kraepelinian tradition, yielding what has been aptly described as "a clinical construct nowhere to be found."
This critical review argues that irritability and psychomotor agitation should be reconsidered as central diagnostic features of mixed depression.
The current specifier's failure to capture diagnostically relevant mixed states has significant implications for patient safety and treatment outcomes and warrants nosological revision.
Consider a patient who presents as depressed but simultaneously paces the hallway, expresses irritability, and reports racing thoughts.
A clinician familiar with mixed presentations will recognize the clinical picture, yet without three or more co-occurring symptoms of the opposite pole, the DSM-5 does not.
Under its restrictive criteria, this patient carries a diagnosis of pure major depressive disorder (MDD)-a categorization that may be clinically misleading and therapeutically consequential.
The misdiagnosis of bipolar depression as unipolar depression has been estimated to occur in up to 60% of patients in its initial presentation (Cardoso et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The misdiagnosis of bipolar depression as unipolar depression has been estimated to occur in up to 60% of patients in its initial presentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cardoso et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A recent study found that 14.5% of patients initially diagnosed with MDD were subsequently diagnosed with bipolar disorder (Wu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A recent study found that 14.5% of patients initially diagnosed with MDD were subsequently diagnosed with bipolar disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Wu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, previous studies have reported that up to 69% of bipolar disorder (BD) patients had previously been misdiagnosed, with consequent delays in appropriate treatment initiation (Hirschfeld et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Moreover, previous studies have reported that up to 69% of bipolar disorder (BD) patients had previously been misdiagnosed, with consequent delays in appropriate treatment initiation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Hirschfeld et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In a longitudinal study following children with prepubertal MDD, nearly 50% of participants were subsequently diagnosed with bipolar disorder (Geller et al., 2001).
text.formatted: In a longitudinal study following children with prepubertal MDD, nearly 50% of participants were subsequently diagnosed with bipolar disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Geller et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore the clinical stakes: because bipolar disorder is frequently misdiagnosed as MDD, the accurate identification of mixed symptom features is important for treatment planning.
This diagnostic gap carries direct consequences; misdiagnosis has been associated with increased rates of substance use, suicide attempts, and psychiatric hospitalization (Goldberg et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This diagnostic gap carries direct consequences; misdiagnosis has been associated with increased rates of substance use, suicide attempts, and psychiatric hospitalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Goldberg et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As the following historical review suggests, these rates of misdiagnosis are not inevitable-they reflect, in part, the departure from a diagnostic tradition that once accommodated precisely this kind of clinical complexity.
German psychiatrist Emil Kraepelin conceptualized mixed states as the simultaneous expression of opposite polarities across three domains: mood, ideation, and volition.
He recognized that these domains need not remain within the same polarity; each could independently manifest at either pole, producing a mixed state.
Kraepelin considered mixed states a fundamental feature of manic-depressive illness (Takeshima & Oka, 2014).
text.formatted: Kraepelin considered mixed states a fundamental feature of manic-depressive illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Takeshima & Oka, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In 1980, the DSM-III artificially bifurcated Kraepelin's unified manic-depressive illness into separate bipolar and unipolar categories, establishing a nosology that departed substantially from Kraepelinian tradition (Koukopoulos et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In 1980, the DSM-III artificially bifurcated Kraepelin's unified manic-depressive illness into separate bipolar and unipolar categories, establishing a nosology that departed substantially from Kraepelinian tradition <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Koukopoulos et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: By making polarity the central axis of diagnosis, the DSM-III rendered mixed states diagnostically rare through the imposition of narrow, non-overlapping criteria.

The DSM-IV-TR required simultaneous fulfillment of full criteria for both a manic and a major depressive episode to meet the threshold for a "mixed episode"-a bar rarely achieved in clinical practice.

The DSM-5 represented a meaningful conceptual advance by replacing the mixed episode diagnosis with a "mixed features specifier" requiring only three or more symptoms of the opposite pole, rather than full syndromal criteria for both poles simultaneously (Takeshima & Oka, 2014).
text.formatted: The DSM-5 represented a meaningful conceptual advance by replacing the mixed episode diagnosis with a "mixed features specifier" requiring only three or more symptoms of the opposite pole, rather than full syndromal criteria for both poles simultaneously <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Takeshima & Oka, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this progress, the DSM-5 Work Group excluded irritability, psychomotor agitation, and distractibility from the specifier's symptom list, reasoning that these features are non-specific and may occur in pure depressive episodes.
This decision produced what Koukopoulos, Sani, and Ghaemi (2013, p. 4) termed "a clinical construct nowhere to be found."

Their critique was direct: excluding psychomotor agitation and irritability while retaining euphoric mood as a qualifying criterion contradicts clinical observation and yields criteria of inadequate prevalence.

The prevalence implications are striking. Koukopoulos et al. (2013) noted that only 0-12% of depressed patients satisfied DSM-5 criteria for mixed features, compared with 33-47% when Koukopoulos' broader criteria-including agitation-were applied. Verdolini et al. (2015) characterized this paradox as the most widespread and substantive criticism of the DSM-5 mixed features specifier: the very exclusion of overlapping symptoms such as psychomotor agitation, irritability, and distractibility-in the name of diagnostic specificity-reduced the specifier's diagnostic power.
text.formatted: The prevalence implications are striking. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Koukopoulos et al. (2013)</ref> noted that only 0-12% of depressed patients satisfied DSM-5 criteria for mixed features, compared with 33-47% when Koukopoulos' broader criteria-including agitation-were applied. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Verdolini et al. (2015)</ref> characterized this paradox as the most widespread and substantive criticism of the DSM-5 mixed features specifier: the very exclusion of overlapping symptoms such as psychomotor agitation, irritability, and distractibility-in the name of diagnostic specificity-reduced the specifier's diagnostic power.

text.text: Benazzi's broader operationalization of mixed depression, which incorporated all symptoms excluded by the DSM-5, demonstrated substantially greater sensitivity for detecting mixed states.
In a direct comparison, Takeshima and Oka (2014) identified mixed symptoms in 16 out of 124 MDD patients using Benazzi's criteria versus zero using the DSM-5 specifier.
text.formatted: In a direct comparison, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Takeshima and Oka (2014)</ref> identified mixed symptoms in 16 out of 124 MDD patients using Benazzi's criteria versus zero using the DSM-5 specifier.

text.text: The DSM-5's exclusion of irritability and psychomotor agitation yielded a 0% detection rate in this MDD sample-raising the question of whether the specifier measures constructs peripheral to the clinical phenomenon it purports to capture.
In this sample, DSM-5 defined mixed criteria identified only 0-7.6% of patients with bipolar depression (Takeshima & Oka, 2014).
text.formatted: In this sample, DSM-5 defined mixed criteria identified only 0-7.6% of patients with bipolar depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Takeshima & Oka, 2014</ref>).

text.text: Benazzi's own studies help explain this gap. Benazzi (2004) found that major depressive episodes accompanied by psychic tension (irritability) and crowded thoughts yielded the highest rate of mixed depression (38.6%), with 76.9% of those cases belonging to the bipolar II spectrum, and reported that combinations of irritability, agitation, and crowded thoughts were significantly associated with external validators of bipolarity.
text.formatted: Benazzi's own studies help explain this gap. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Benazzi (2004)</ref> found that major depressive episodes accompanied by psychic tension (irritability) and crowded thoughts yielded the highest rate of mixed depression (38.6%), with 76.9% of those cases belonging to the bipolar II spectrum, and reported that combinations of irritability, agitation, and crowded thoughts were significantly associated with external validators of bipolarity.

text.text: In a larger study, Benazzi (2005) identified agitated depression in 34.7% of depressed outpatients; 70.1% of these cases were classified as mixed, supporting a link to the bipolar spectrum while suggesting that psychomotor agitation alone, without additional concurrent symptoms, may be insufficient to define agitated depression as a discrete diagnostic subtype.
text.formatted: In a larger study, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Benazzi (2005)</ref> identified agitated depression in 34.7% of depressed outpatients; 70.1% of these cases were classified as mixed, supporting a link to the bipolar spectrum while suggesting that psychomotor agitation alone, without additional concurrent symptoms, may be insufficient to define agitated depression as a discrete diagnostic subtype.

text.text: Taken together, these findings indicate that the very symptoms the DSM-5 excludes are among those most consistently associated with markers of bipolarity.

Evidence on the prevalence of these excluded symptoms in clinical populations reinforces this conclusion. Judd et al. (2012) found that irritability and psychomotor agitation were the most prevalent subsyndromal manic symptoms during bipolar major depressive episodes, co-occurring in 57% and 39% of episodes, respectively, and accounting for most negative prognostic effects, including longer episode duration and elevated suicidality.
text.formatted: Evidence on the prevalence of these excluded symptoms in clinical populations reinforces this conclusion. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Judd et al. (2012)</ref> found that irritability and psychomotor agitation were the most prevalent subsyndromal manic symptoms during bipolar major depressive episodes, co-occurring in 57% and 39% of episodes, respectively, and accounting for most negative prognostic effects, including longer episode duration and elevated suicidality.

text.text: At the individual symptom level, a study of 93 patients with MDD found that those who were irritable demonstrated higher rates of bipolar family history, hypomanic episodes, and mixed states compared with non-irritable depressed patients (Parneix et al., 2014); as approximately one-third of patients with an MDD diagnosis report clinically significant irritability, current criteria appear to miss a meaningful subgroup exhibiting markers of bipolarity. Sani et al. (2022) further confirmed that depressive and manic symptom severity in mixed depression was significantly associated with distractibility, irritability, and agitation-as well as anxiety, which exerted particularly strong influence on overall severity in that sample. Fagiolini et al. (2015) arrived at a similar conclusion, identifying irritability, agitation, and anxiety as the prominent features of mixed states-precisely the symptoms excluded by the DSM-5.

(2015)</ref> arrived at a similar conclusion, identifying irritability, agitation, and anxiety as the prominent features of mixed states-precisely the symptoms excluded by the DSM-5.

text.text: The problems extend beyond the symptom list to the measurement tools used to operationalize it. Zimmerman et al. (2023) documented an eight-fold variation in the prevalence of mixed features depending on the diagnostic instrument employed, arising from poor agreement between Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS)-based definitions and the DSM-5 Mixed Features Specifier Interview (DMSI).

(2023)</ref> documented an eight-fold variation in the prevalence of mixed features depending on the diagnostic instrument employed, arising from poor agreement between Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS)-based definitions and the DSM-5 Mixed Features Specifier Interview (DMSI).

text.text: 3.9%), suggesting that the current threshold may systematically miss patients whose mixed symptoms fluctuate over time.

The phenomenological heterogeneity observed in clinical practice compounds this further. Perugi et al. (1997), in a study of 143 mixed state patients, found that only 54% met DSM-III-R criteria for mixed states-corresponding to the narrower category of dysphoric mixed mania.

(1997)</ref>, in a study of 143 mixed state patients, found that only 54% met DSM-III-R criteria for mixed states-corresponding to the narrower category of dysphoric mixed mania.

text.text: Of the remainder, 17.5% were characterized by irritable mood and flight of ideas consistent with mixed agitated psychotic depressive states, and 26% presented with fatigue and indecisiveness in a pattern described as unproductive-inhibited mania.

This distribution underscores that the majority of clinically recognized mixed presentations fall outside the boundaries of criteria anchored to euphoric or dysphoric mania, reinforcing the argument that current diagnostic thresholds may systematically underrepresent the most common mixed state subtypes.

The three-symptom threshold for the mixed features specifier lacks a clearly established empirical basis and may reduce the sensitivity of the diagnosis by excluding patients with diagnostically relevant symptoms of opposite polarity.

Consistent with this concern, the multinational BRIDGE-II-MIX study found that broader research-based criteria identified depressed mixed states in 29.1% of patients, substantially exceeding rates obtained using DSM-5 criteria and suggesting that restrictive thresholds may underestimate the prevalence of mixed presentations (Perugi et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Consistent with this concern, the multinational BRIDGE-II-MIX study found that broader research-based criteria identified depressed mixed states in 29.1% of patients, substantially exceeding rates obtained using DSM-5 criteria and suggesting that restrictive thresholds may underestimate the prevalence of mixed presentations <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Perugi et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A comparison of seven different approaches to assessing mixed features in 309 depressed patients revealed a prevalence range with an eight-fold difference between methods (Zimmerman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A comparison of seven different approaches to assessing mixed features in 309 depressed patients revealed a prevalence range with an eight-fold difference between methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Zimmerman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of concordance among standardized instruments highlights the limitations of the current operational framework and calls into question the empirical grounding of the threshold itself.

Categorical diagnostic thresholds, such as those employed by the DSM, tend to inadequately capture symptom severity and dimensionality. Craddock et al. (2004) identified several limitations of categorical nosology, including arbitrary boundaries between diagnostic categories, excessive reliance on subjective clinical interpretation, loss of clinically meaningful information through hierarchical exclusion rules, and the inability to accommodate subsyndromal presentations.
text.formatted: Categorical diagnostic thresholds, such as those employed by the DSM, tend to inadequately capture symptom severity and dimensionality. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Craddock et al. (2004)</ref> identified several limitations of categorical nosology, including arbitrary boundaries between diagnostic categories, excessive reliance on subjective clinical interpretation, loss of clinically meaningful information through hierarchical exclusion rules, and the inability to accommodate subsyndromal presentations.

text.text: A dimensional approach offers a more clinically sensitive alternative by accommodating subsyndromal features and capturing severity gradations that categorical thresholds cannot.

The Bipolar Affective Disorder Dimension Scale (BADDS), which rates lifetime psychopathology across four dimensions-mania, depression, psychosis, and incongruence-has demonstrated high inter-rater reliability while preserving diagnostic information (Craddock et al., 2004).
text.formatted: The Bipolar Affective Disorder Dimension Scale (BADDS), which rates lifetime psychopathology across four dimensions-mania, depression, psychosis, and incongruence-has demonstrated high inter-rater reliability while preserving diagnostic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Craddock et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, the Bipolarity Index, at a cut-off score of 50 or above, demonstrated high sensitivity (0.91) and specificity (0.90) for distinguishing bipolar disorder from MDD in a recent meta-analysis, supporting dimensional approaches over categorical ones (Zhang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, the Bipolarity Index, at a cut-off score of 50 or above, demonstrated high sensitivity (0.91) and specificity (0.90) for distinguishing bipolar disorder from MDD in a recent meta-analysis, supporting dimensional approaches over categorical ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Zhang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This contemporary approach to mood classification is consistent with a return to Kraepelinian principles, evaluating psychopathology along a continuum rather than within discrete, mutually exclusive categories.
The limitations of the DSM-5 mixed features specifier are broadly recognized within the psychiatric literature.

A systematic review by Verdolini et al. (2015) identified the exclusion of irritability, psychomotor agitation, and distractibility as the most frequent and substantive criticism raised by clinicians and researchers alike.
text.formatted: A systematic review by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Verdolini et al. (2015)</ref> identified the exclusion of irritability, psychomotor agitation, and distractibility as the most frequent and substantive criticism raised by clinicians and researchers alike.

text.text: Proposed remedies include broadening the qualifying symptom list to incorporate excluded features, lowering the three-symptom threshold for subsyndromal presentations, and adopting a spectrum-based rather than categorical approachdevelopments that would align the specifier more closely with Kraepelinian principles (Verdolini et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Proposed remedies include broadening the qualifying symptom list to incorporate excluded features, lowering the three-symptom threshold for subsyndromal presentations, and adopting a spectrum-based rather than categorical approachdevelopments that would align the specifier more closely with Kraepelinian principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Verdolini et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Patients with subsyndromal presentations-those exhibiting one or two mixed symptoms, agitated depression, or cyclothymic temperament-display treatment response patterns consistent with underlying bipolarity that current criteria fail to capture. Koukopoulos et al. (2013) and others have advocated for mixed depression to be accorded independent diagnostic status within the DSM, or for the abandonment of discrete categories in favor of a mood spectrum model.
text.formatted: Patients with subsyndromal presentations-those exhibiting one or two mixed symptoms, agitated depression, or cyclothymic temperament-display treatment response patterns consistent with underlying bipolarity that current criteria fail to capture. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Koukopoulos et al. (2013)</ref> and others have advocated for mixed depression to be accorded independent diagnostic status within the DSM, or for the abandonment of discrete categories in favor of a mood spectrum model.

text.text: Future nosological revisions should consider treating agitation and irritability as central, rather than exclusionary, features of the diagnostic construct.

Until such revisions are implemented, clinicians would be well served to look beyond the DSM-5 specifier to identify patients at elevated risk for bipolar disorder, poor antidepressant response, and treatmentemergent mania.
Several limitations of this critical review warrant acknowledgment.

First, the present synthesis, while comprehensive, does not constitute a formal systematic review with structured quality assessment; such a review would strengthen the evidence base for nosological revision.

Second, much of the foundational evidence derives from Western populations, and cross-cultural validation of mixed features presentations is needed to ensure that revised diagnostic criteria have global applicability.

Third, critiquing current criteria is not equivalent to proposing validated alternatives; the development and prospective validation of alternative diagnostic algorithms will require large-scale studies with methodological consistency.
Fourth, optimal pharmacological strategies for mixed depression remain uncertain owing to the paucity of randomized controlled trials using consistent diagnostic criteria.
Future research should prioritize adequately powered trials comparing mood stabilizers, second-generation antipsychotics, and combination regimens in well-characterized mixed depression populations.

Finally, the development of biomarkers and neuroimaging measures may ultimately provide objective complements to clinical symptom assessment, reducing reliance on subjective report and threshold-dependent categorization.
A central concern emerging from this review is that the DSM-5 mixed features specifier excludes the very symptoms that most consistently characterize mixed depression.
The result may be a diagnostic construct that underidentifies the patients who most urgently need accurate classification.

Multiple independent lines of evidence suggest that patients with agitated depression present with irritable mood, psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, flight of ideas, and in some cases psychotic symptoms-features that represent a clinically severe variant of bipolar depression (Benazzi, 2005; Maj et al., 2003; Perugi et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Multiple independent lines of evidence suggest that patients with agitated depression present with irritable mood, psychomotor agitation, pressured speech, flight of ideas, and in some cases psychotic symptoms-features that represent a clinically severe variant of bipolar depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Benazzi, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Maj et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Perugi et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Until nosological revisions formally integrate agitation and irritability as central diagnostic features of mixed depression, clinicians may find it necessary to look beyond the DSM-5's restrictive specifier to identify patients who carry the burden of a mixed presentation without the diagnostic recognition that should accompany it.
